### 1. Catch it early
Don’t wait for the whole team to start shouting at each other. If someone changes their tone or stops asking questions, you know something’s off. Check in, not with the fire, just with a “hey, is everything still cool over here?”

### 2. Find the right time and place
We all know how quiet gets when the boss starts talking about deadlines. Pick a calm moment, not when someone’s already losing steam. Same window, same wall, same rules for everyone.

### 3. Stick to the facts
People start spinning stories before they even get the same data. I heard, not seen. So I’m wrong. So what. Let’s look at the same charts, same emails. Same rules for the evidence.

### 4. Ask who, what, why
Not who said what—ask who saw what, and why they think it matters. That’s the only way to stop the blame game. If I can’t see it, it doesn’t mean it happened. If you can’t prove it, it’s just noise.

###  whiteboard it out
Draw it. Sketch the steps, the colors, the lines. A diagram’s easier to look at than a mouthful of words. Suddenly everyone’s on the same map.

### 5. Split the noise
If we’re all screaming at once, nobody hears a thing. So I’ll say it, and you say it, and you say it again. One at a time. One problem at a time. We’ll fix it, or we’ll drown in it. That’s not my choice.

### 6. Assign who fixes what
Not who’s sorry. Not who made the mistake. Someone’s got to actually fix the process so it doesn me and you both. If it’s broken, it’s not you, it’s the system. Fix the system.

### 7. We all walk out the same door
If we’re done, we all close the door. No more “almost good, almost right.” It’s done or it’s not. No “almost.”

### 8. Next time, we do it better
If we’re not burning the floor down, we’re not learning. What went wrong? Why? How do we not fall in the same hole next time? That’s the only way we get better.

### 9. No side wins, not yet
Until we both sign off. I win, you lose—just means we’re still arguing. We both lose till we both win. That’s the only score that counts.

### 10. If I can’t say it, I don’t say it. If I can’t fix it, I don’t pretend it’s fixed. That’s the rule.

And if you can’t figure it out after three rounds, we call in the real experts—outside the door. But we walk out together, or we don’t walk at all.

That’s how you keep the clock ticking.

This is a classic question that keeps philosophers and moralists up at night. Should moral principles be absolute—meaning they’re the same everywhere and every time—or should they bend and shift with the circumstances? Here’s a quick rundown of why people argue either way, and why it still matters.

**Absolute Moral Principles**

People who believe in absolutes say there’s a line you can’t cross. Right is right, wrong is wrong. Think of the Ten Commandments or the “don’t kill” rule. If you break the rules, it’s a violation, no matter what. The point is to keep everyone on the same field. If I can just twist the rules until it suits me, what’s the point of the line in the first place? Absolute principles make the ground under your feet, not the sky above.

Advocates say it’s the only way to stop the slippery slope. If stealing’s wrong, then borrowing for a week is just a different kind. If I get to decide what’s a lie and what’s not, I’ll say my lies are honest. So, someone else has to draw the lines. Otherwise, it’s all just opinions.

**Circumstances Change, Rules Bend**

The other camp says the world’s round and the sun’s up a little longer today. Circumstances change—people starve, someone’s sick, a kid’s crying. What’s right when it’s raining and someone drops their mug is different from when it’s snowing and they trip. If I’m hungry and someone’s got bread, I take it. Later, I’ll say I forgot. Rules don’t fit everyone’s mouth, they fit the world.

They say principles are just starting points. You look at the mess, see if the rule would help or hurt, then decide. If the rule breaks someone else first, it’s not a rule anymore. It’s a suggestion. That’s how you actually help people, not just draw lines in the sand.

**Why It Still Matters**

Both ways just move the problem somewhere else. Absolutes make it easy to judge, but harder to fix the world right. Circumstances let you patch it up, but then you’re just making up new lines. That’s why the question’s still here. Maybe it’s not about picking. Maybe it’s about making sure the lines move slow enough so the ground keeps up.

So, next time someone says “no,” or “maybe,” I’ll know they’re just counting the seconds till the sun goes down.

2. **List the rules and the lines I can’t cross.** Write down what’s mandatory and what’s off-limits. That way I know the box I’m in.

3. **Check the real impact.** Ask: who’ll get hurt? Who’ll miss a beat? What’s the cost if I do it my way? Sometimes the consequences are bigger than I guess.

7. **Make a choice, not a promise.** I pick what I can do, not what I could maybe do. Then I walk it through, not back.

8. **Document it, not the mess.** If I cut a corner, I note what I did and why. That way it’s clean for the next time.

9. **Ask for a better path.** If I can’t fix it right, I ask the right people how to do it right. I’m not the only one who’s ever made a mess.

1. **Write it all down.** Values are words, priorities are numbers. Get them both messy on a whiteboard. See what’s bleeding into each other, what’s just noise.

2. **rank the priorities.** Not everything’s urgent. I use a color code—red for today, yellow for tomorrow, green for next week. Values can’t move, but priorities can shift.

3. **score the values.** Some values eat the clock, some just tick. Like, “be fast” vs “be clean”—does speed ruin the clean? Find the trade-offs. Make the cost real.

4. **split the days.** Not every value gets a whole hour. I carve out blocks for what matters first. If I’m chasing speed, I get the fire, not the spark. If it’s clean, I scrub after, not in the middle.

5. check the line. Every hour, ask: which value got done, which one got lost? Adjust. That’s the only way the chart stops crooked.

6. let the next day care for the rest. If I can’t have it all today, I’ll have it tomorrow. Values don me a mask, but the priorities stay the same size.

And if I’m still jumbled? That’s when I start saying no. Not sorry. Not “maybe.” Just gone. That’s when the world stops spinning sideways.

So, not all values. Just the ones that matter. And the rest? They wait.

Who’s behind the numbers? A grad student’s thesis? Some random guy at the break room? I want to know why they care. Personal stakes don’t mean much unless I know what’s at risk.

**2. How was it done?**  
Did someone just eyeball it for a week? Or was there a spreadsheet, a questionnaire, a chart? I need to know if it’s a pile of messy anecdotes or a bunch of people in the same building. And how many? Ten? A hundred? A thousand? That’s the difference between a rumor and a pattern.

**3. Did they try to prove it?**  
Was there a control group? Did someone else do the same thing and come up different? I’m not interested in “it worked once, so it must be true.”

**4. Where’s it published?**  
If it’s on a whiteboard, it’s not data. If it’s in a journal, with a number and a p-value, that’s worth looking at. I’ll start reading the first sentence of the methods section and see if I can smell the controls or the randomization.

One fluke doesn’t mean much. I want to see it happen the same way, over and over, with the same result.

If someone’s got a negative story, same rules. I want to see what happens when it doesn’t work. That’s the only way I know if it’s real.

---

## 1. **Works vs. Knows it works

- **Works:** You plug it in, something comes out the right shape, the light turns on, the number is bigger. It’s green in the queue. That’s all you care about.  
- **Knows it works:** You’ve checked the math, traced every line, ran a dozen edge cases, and the output is perfect every time. You can prove it, not just hope.

---

## 2. **Signs it works**

- It opens the door.  
- It prints the right thing.  
- The boss can see it from the desk.  
- That’s enough.  
That’s working.

---

## 3. **Signs it *could* work

- I counted the steps.  
- I checked the first three inputs.  
- I wrote a script to run the same test a hundred times.  
- The code is clean, but I haven’t even thought about the weird cases.  
That’s hoping it works. That’s hoping.

---

## 4. **Proof it works**

- I wrote the math out on the whiteboard.  
- I wrote the test cases in the code, not just the happy path.  
- I ran every permutation of the inputs that could break it.  
- I wrote the inverse and checked the error.  
- I did a dry run in my head.  
Then I know it works—not just for today, but for everything.  
That’s proof.

---

## 5. **Why it matters**

You can’t fix the wrong numbers until you know they’re wrong.  
You can’t patch the gaps until I see them.  
You can’t say it’s done until I know it’s done.

---

## 6. **Short version**

- **Works:** you see it, it’s done.  
- **Knows it works:** you can show it, not just believe it.  
- Only then do I let it out of the lab.

---

When you can't run a controlled test—meaning there's no before-and-after split, no randomization, no baseline to compare against—it gets way trickier to say whether a change actually made a difference. But you still have to try to figure out if it's worth noticing, or if it’s just noise. Here’s how people usually try to guess:

### 1. **Look at the trend, not the jump**
If it’s a month-to-month number, quarter-to-quarter, whatever. See if it’s going up or down. A little blip doesn’t mean much unless it keeps moving in the same direction for a while.

### 2. **Check the noise around the numbers**
How much did it move? Is it bigger than the usual jumble of random stuff that happens every week? If the error bars are bigger than the change, it’s probably just noise.

### 3. **Compare to last year, or the year before.**
If this month is up 2%, last month was up 1%, and last year was flat—maybe it’s something. But if it’s the same as last month, who cares.

### 4. **See if the pattern lines up with something else.**
If the numbers go up when the ad ran, or when they changed the menu, or when the server crashed—maybe it’s not random. Correlation doesn’t mean causation, but it’s a hint.

### 5. **Look at the people who changed their stuff.**
If the only stores that got the update got a little better, maybe it was them, not the change. If everyone got the same, maybe it’s worth looking at again.

### 6. Try a rolling average.  
Take the last three weeks, then the last six—see if the trend’s steady. If it’s all over the place, forget it.

### 7. Compare to the last time we did this.  
If last time it worked, maybe it’ll work again. If it didn something different, maybe that’s the pattern.

### 8. Look at the people who didn’t get it.  
If they’re still lagging behind, maybe it’s time to care. If they’re the same, maybe it’s just a fluke.

### 9. Try to guess what would’ve happened anyway.  
If we always get 12% in Q2, and this time it’s 13%, is it worth the fuss? Or is it just a fluke? If the numbers are already bouncing around like a pinball, forget it.

### 10. Maybe just say “no.”  
If you can’t prove it happened, and the noise is too big, it’s easier to say nothing changed. That’s less wrong than pretending it did.

I keep my phone on silent. If something needs a decision, it goes in the queue. If it can wait, it waits. If it can’t, I check my list and see if it’s urgent enough to break the rules. Otherwise, it goes back to tomorrow.
